notes.5-1283:
Binary search on the divisor from `1` to `max(nums)`.

For every guessed divisor `mid`, calculate:

```cpp
sum += (num + mid - 1) / mid;
```

This is the integer version of:

```cpp
ceil((double)num / mid)
```

Then compare the calculated `sum` with `threshold`.

* If `sum <= threshold`, the divisor works. Set `r = mid`, not `mid - 1`, because we need the smallest valid divisor and `mid` itself may be the answer.
* If `sum > threshold`, the divisor is too small. Smaller divisors will produce an even larger sum, so discard the left half using `l = mid + 1`.

When `l == r`, both pointers are at the smallest valid divisor, so return `l`.

notes.9-739: Use a monotonic decreasing stack of indices. Each index in the stack represents a previous day still waiting for a warmer temperature. While the current temperature is greater than the temperature at the stack’s top index, pop that index and set its answer as currentIndex - previousIndex. Then push the current index. Any indices left in the stack at the end have no warmer future day, so their answer remains 0. Time complexity is O(n) because every index is pushed and popped at most once.

notes.11-692: In #692, count words using unordered_map<string,int>, then push them into a heap as {frequency, word}, so the heap uses pair<int,string>. The custom comparator returns true when a should have lower priority than b: a.first < b.first makes lower-frequency words go below higher-frequency ones, and if frequencies are equal, a.second > b.second makes lexicographically larger words go below smaller ones. Thus the heap top is always the highest-frequency word, and on a tie, the dictionary-smaller word comes first.

notes.12-57: For LeetCode 57 – Insert Interval, since the given intervals are already sorted and non-overlapping, we traverse them once while carrying the new interval using start and end. There are three cases: if the current interval ends before start, it is completely before the new interval so we directly push it; if it starts after end, it is completely after, so we first insert the merged {start, end} once and then push the remaining intervals; otherwise, the intervals overlap, so we merge using start = min(start, intervals[i][0]) and end = max(end, intervals[i][1]). The main mistakes are inserting the new interval multiple times, forgetting to merge across several consecutive overlaps, or forgetting to insert it at the end if no later interval triggers the “after” case. Overall complexity is O(n) time and O(n) space for the answer.

notes.12-253: For Meeting Rooms II, sort the start[] and end[] arrays separately and use two pointers. If start[i] < end[j], a new meeting begins before the earliest current meeting ends, so we need another room: increment rooms and update maxRooms. Otherwise, a meeting has finished, so decrement rooms and move the end pointer j. If start[i] == end[j], we can reuse the same room, so it goes to the “meeting ended” case. The answer is the maximum number of rooms used at the same time, because that is the minimum number of rooms required overall. Time complexity is O(n log n) due to sorting, with O(1) extra space apart from sorting.
